notes.meaning: King Sennacherib of Assyria invaded the kingdom of Judah and captured all its fortified cities. God allowed this terrifying crisis to test the faith of King Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem. The invasion fulfilled earlier warnings that Assyrian armies would sweep through the land like an overflowing river.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historians date Sennacherib's campaign to 701 BC and suggest Hezekiah had a coregency, or that the date of the fourteenth year was originally connected to Hezekiah's illness in chapter 38.

notes.meaning: Sennacherib sent his chief officer, the Rabshakeh, along with a massive army from the besieged city of Lachish to Jerusalem. The officer stopped by the aqueduct of the upper pool on the road to the Launderer's Field. This was the exact spot where the prophet Isaiah had confronted Hezekiah's father, Ahaz, challenging him to trust God instead of foreign powers.

Three high-ranking officials came out from the city walls to meet the Assyrian envoy. Eliakim had replaced Shebna as the palace administrator, fulfilling a prophecy Isaiah had given earlier. Together with Shebna, who was demoted to secretary, and Joah the recorder, they carried the heavy burden of hearing the enemy's harsh demands.

The Rabshakeh refused to give Hezekiah the title of king, while boasting that his own master was the emperor, or the great king. He began a war of words meant to terrify the Judean leaders into giving up without a battle. His sharp question challenged the very foundation of their hope.

The Assyrian officer mocked Judah's military plans, calling them empty words with no real power to back them up. He asked who Hezekiah was relying on that gave him the nerve to rebel against the mighty Assyrian empire. His goal was to make Judah's defense look hopeless and foolish.

The Rabshakeh warned that leaning on Egypt was like leaning on a brittle river reed that snaps and pierces a person's hand. He was right that Egypt was a completely useless ally, which was the very warning Isaiah had repeatedly preached. Yet the Assyrian spoke this truth not to turn Judah to the Lord, but to push them into absolute despair.

The Rabshakeh claimed that the people could not trust the Lord because Hezekiah had just destroyed their local altars and shrines. As a pagan who thought gods wanted as many shrines as possible, he completely misunderstood Hezekiah's reforms, which had removed idol worship and centered true worship at the temple in Jerusalem. He craftily tried to make the citizens believe their king had offended God instead of pleasing Him.

The Assyrian envoy mockingly proposed a wager to Hezekiah. He offered to supply two thousand horses if Judah could even produce enough trained soldiers to ride them. This insult drove home how weak Judah's cavalry was compared to Assyria's modern fighting forces.

The Rabshakeh asked how Jerusalem could turn back even the lowest-ranking Assyrian captain when Judah had to beg Egypt for horsemen and chariots. He pointed out the kingdom's complete helplessness in human warfare. He wanted the leaders to feel that surrender was their only logical choice.

The officer audaciously claimed that the Lord God Himself had sent Assyria to wipe out Judah. God was indeed using Assyria to discipline His people, but Sennacherib's army acted out of cruel greed rather than obedience to God. The Rabshakeh used this claim to shake the faith of the Judean officials and make them feel that resisting Assyria was fighting against God.

Hezekiah's officials pleaded with the Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, the common language of international diplomacy. They asked him not to speak in Hebrew because the soldiers and people standing on the city wall could understand it. The officials were terrified that hearing the enemy's threats would cause the people to lose heart and panic.

The Rabshakeh crudely replied that his message was meant directly for the common men guarding the wall. He warned that if they stayed loyal to Hezekiah through a long siege, they would starve until they were forced to consume their own body waste. His graphic words were intended to break the soldiers' spirits and spark a mutiny.

Recognizing the fear among Hezekiah's officials, the Rabshakeh stood tall and raised his voice to shout in Hebrew. He commanded all the citizens within earshot to listen to the words of the great king of Assyria. This was a direct appeal over the heads of the city's leaders to provoke surrender.

The Assyrian messenger warned the people on the wall not to let Hezekiah trick them with promises of deliverance. He insisted that their king had no power to save them from Assyria's overwhelming might. He sought to tear away the citizens' trust in their godly ruler.

The Rabshakeh knew that Hezekiah's true defense was his strong faith in God, so he attacked that trust directly. He told the citizens not to believe their king when he assured them that the Lord would step in and rescue Jerusalem. He understood that if he could destroy their faith in God, the city would fall without a fight.

The officer urged the people to ignore Hezekiah and make peace with the king of Assyria by surrendering. He promised that each person would be allowed to eat from his own grapevine and fig tree and drink from his own cistern. He dressed up defeat as a peaceful and comfortable life to tempt them into giving up.

The Rabshakeh admitted that Sennacherib would eventually deport them to a faraway country, but he promised it would be just as fruitful as Judah. He painted forced exile as an appealing move to a land of grain, bread, and vineyards. In reality, he was glossing over the cruel Assyrian practice of uprooting conquered nations from their homeland.

The Assyrian commander crossed the line into open blasphemy by comparing the Lord to man-made idols. He boldly asked whether the god of any conquered nation had ever managed to rescue its land from Assyria's king. He viewed Israel's God as merely another local deity who would easily be crushed.

The Rabshakeh rattled off a list of defeated cities and pointed out that their gods had vanished into Assyrian temples as war trophies. He pointedly asked if any god had delivered Samaria, the northern kingdom of Israel, from Assyrian conquest. To him, the fall of Samaria proved that Jerusalem's God had no power to save Judah.

The Rabshakeh concluded that since no other god had rescued its land from Assyria, the Lord could not save Jerusalem either. By treating the Creator of the universe like a helpless wooden idol, he insulted God directly. This arrogant blasphemy turned the war into a contest between Sennacherib and the living God.

The people on the wall kept completely silent and did not speak a single word in reply. King Hezekiah had given strict orders not to answer the enemy's insults. Refusing to argue showed wise self-control and protected the people from being pulled into a shouting match with a mocking blasphemer.

Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah tore their clothes and returned to King Hezekiah to report everything the Rabshakeh had said. Tearing their clothes was a traditional sign of deep sorrow and horror at hearing God blasphemed. In their grief and helplessness, they brought the crisis directly to their king and prepared to seek the Lord.
